title: Evening prayer
hookLine: Jacob's prayer, said as night falls

cards: A young man is running away from home. He's fooled his father, and his brother wants him dead. He walks until the sun sets on the road to Haran: nowhere to sleep, no inn, no tent.
He puts a stone under his head and lies down in the open. That night he'll dream of a ladder with angels on it. But before the dream, there's a small verb in the text that the rabbis noticed.
And from that verb, they found the evening prayer.

teach.b: Genesis, in the old Jewish translation: "And he lighted upon the place, and tarried there all night, because the sun was set." Lighted upon, in Hebrew vayifga: he came upon, he met, he ran into.
The Talmud, in Berakhot, says that same verb can mean to plead or to pray, and reads it here as prayer.
So Abraham has the morning, Isaac the afternoon, and Jacob, alone on the road at sundown, the night.

The evening prayer is called Maariv, from its first blessing, which praises God who brings on the evenings, ma'ariv aravim. Some communities call it Arvit, from the same root, evening. Now a surprising piece of history.
The Talmud records an argument about whether the evening prayer was required at all.

One sage said it was optional; another, an obligation. There's a well-known, tense story of the academy's leaders clashing over it. In time, it became a fixed part of every day, but a trace of the argument is still there.
At Maariv, the leader doesn't repeat the Amidah aloud, the way they do in the morning and afternoon. Everyone says it silently, and the service moves on. One more detail.
The Talmud ties the morning and afternoon prayers to the Temple's two daily offerings. For the night, it can only point to what was left burning on the altar until morning.
There was no evening offering of its own. Just, in the story, a person on a road, meeting the place where he stopped.

how: Maariv is said after nightfall: Barchu, the Shema with its blessings, and the Amidah said silently without a repetition aloud, followed by Aleinu; many people say it right after Mincha, near sunset.

games.q: you're leading the evening service. everyone has finished the silent Amidah. what comes next?
o: repeat the whole Amidah aloud, as in the morning.
games.why: at Maariv there's no repetition aloud, a trace of the old argument that evening prayer was optional.

practice: Wherever you'll be when the light goes, that's your place, the way the roadside was Jacob's; look outside if it's dark, or picture this evening's sunset, and slowly notice the room, the street, the sky.
If you pray, offer an evening prayer in any words you have; if not, just meet the place you've landed.

wordCard.voice: Maariv. The one who brings on evening. The night prayer, traced to Jacob meeting the place at sunset.

orig.note: Hebrew: bringing on the evening. the name of the night prayer.

carryVoice: Your line: meet the place you've landed. Even a roadside can be the place. Until tomorrow.
